chapter_theme: General songs (பொதுப்பாடல்கள், 18 of 21): the poet asks to be lifted above the quarrels of sects and the lure of women, out of the body seen as self and the bubble of life, and to be given the true word, the teaching Murugan gave Siva, and the feet; one song is a love-lament, one a vow that in kingship or poverty he will speak only of the feet, and one a frank account of love answered by a plea for Vedanta's lamp.
structure_note: Several songs ask for a word or teaching rather than escape alone: 1247 (the Lord beyond he, she and it), 1248, 1251, 1252, 1253 and 1261. Women are the confession of 1248, 1256 to 1261; the body and its end of 1250. 1249 is a vision of union at the Sivaganga tank; 1254 an akam lament in the girl's voice; 1255 a vow. 1251 has the ghost-troupe singing Thiruppugazh itself.

1247.reading: The poet asks whether he, a lonely one, will come to know the Lord whose form passes beyond both form and the formless and beyond all talk of he, she and it, without being drawn into dispute with the blind who left the path of austerity, the hair-plucking ascetics, ritualists and sectarians of many kinds. The praise shows the earth shaken, the northern peak shattered, the serpent king's crests crushed and the ancient sea dried as Murugan answers the appeal of the gods' king and turns the demon army to dust, riding the dancing emerald steed.
1247.nuance: அவன் இவன் உவன் உடன் அவள் இவள் உவள் அது இது உது எனும் ஆறு அற்று: the Lord is beyond the threefold grammar of person and distance, a formula that also opens Saiva and Vaishnava doctrinal works. தலைபறி, those who pluck out their hair, are Jain ascetics; பரபாதத் தருமிகள் is less clear. The plea is not to defeat the sects but to stop quarrelling (சருவா நின்று) and know.

1248.reading: The poet describes the breasts of women, likened to the tusks of rutting elephants, to radiant peaks and to tender coconuts, and the creeper-like women who exhaust young men, and asks that the nights and days he spends in their net end and he be set to praise Murugan. The praise names him the one who first told the subtle, supreme truth to Brahma, Vishnu and Siva who did not know it, the vel that struck the rakshasa hiding in the sea, and the companion of great poets who find the best word in an instant.
1248.nuance: சததள பார்த்திபற்கு அரி புருஷோத்தமற்கு எரிகனல் ஏற்றவற்கு: Brahma of the hundred-petalled lotus, Vishnu and Siva who holds fire all receive the teaching; Om is not named. கவிஞர் உசாத்துணை: Murugan as the poets' confidant, a role the poet claims for his own songs. The Sanskrit compounds of the praise are hard to divide.

1249.reading: The poet asks that, with wrinkles, grey hair, the body's suffering and the two deceitful deeds destroyed, he bathe and play in the Sivaganga tank, that Sivam leap into him so that his inner form becomes Murugan's form, and that, with gods, sages, Brahma and Vishnu calling him Hara's son and Ganapati 'my younger brother', Murugan come on the peacock with the vel, join his father in the holy dance, and give the precious meaning. The praise names Siva, the dancer of Madurai who made foxes into horses for a Pandya king, and Murugan the vel that burns to powder the dark hill, the asuras and our two deeds, who dwells in the poet's love with Valli.
1249.nuance: The plea is a vision, not a confession: bath, possession by Sivam, transformation into the god's form (அக வடிவு உன்றன் வடிவம் என), and the dance. பரி என்ப நரிகள் தமை and மதுரை நடராஜன் name the foxes turned to horses, a Madurai sacred game of Siva. பழியஞ்சி may be the Madurai Siva's name 'who feared blame', and புண்டரிக வடிவ may point to Chidambaram; both are unclear. The same vel burns the asuras and 'our two deeds'.

1250.reading: The poet confesses that, not knowing how to end the great maya that takes as 'I' a leather bag of the five elements oozing the mire of desire, he tends a body that ghosts, vultures, jackals and crows will tear and drag, and asks Murugan to uproot him from this clown's life driven as if by a madman and give his feet. The praise tells of Murugan changing form to court the hunter girl in the bamboo forest, riding the peacock, striking golden Meru to its roots and burning hostile beings to ash to guard heaven.
1250.nuance: தோற்பை யான் ஆக நோக்கும் மா மாயை: the delusion named is taking the body for oneself, not only lust. தீ, உதை, தாத்ரி, பானீயம், வான்: the five elements in mixed Tamil and Sanskrit. பேயோன் நடாத்து கோமாளி வாழ்க்கை, a buffoon's life run by a madman, is the song's sharpest image.

1251.reading: Against sophist sectarians who rise quivering to argue and plant flag against flag, the poet asks to be wholly Murugan's servant and given, without fault, the meaning of the one word that makes plain the first principle unknown to the Vedas. The praise shows a trained troupe of ghosts drinking, dancing and bathing in a sea of blood, smashing hills, and reciting, beginning and ending Thiruppugazh songs, as Murugan crushes the demons in a blink.
1251.nuance: படிப்பன திருப்புகழ் எடுப்பன முடிப்பன: the book names itself, sung by the ghosts of the battlefield. ஒரு மொழிப்பொருள், the meaning of one word, likely points to Om but does not name it. The first half's chain of -ன verbs (துகைப்பன, அறுப்பன, துணிப்பன, விழுப்பன), trampling and cutting heads, is hard to assign: it may describe the poet's victory over the debaters in argument or the vel's work.

1252.reading: The poet lists the adornments of Siva's matted hair (the hooded serpent, jasmine, nochi, vilva, the crescent of nectar, the red patali, golden konrai, the waves of the Ganga, the blue lily, erukku, dhatura) and asks Murugan to give him, whose life is a bubble, the pure true word of weighty wisdom he gave in grace to that Siva. The praise shows Murugan on the peacock, killing the asuras, the sea heaving, Sura as the mango split, Indra's elephant fleeing to hide, and the cock held in his hand.
1252.nuance: புற்புதப் பிராணன், a life like a bubble (budbuda), is the plea's whole self-description, set against the long catalogue of Siva's flowers. வாரணம் returns in the last lines as sea, elephant and cock, a play the rhythm hides. Several flower names and the praise's compounds are uncertain.

1253.reading: Before his heart can grasp the truth about wife, children, wealth and kin, and before fierce, strong ones surround him, kick him with cruel troubles and break his strength, the poet asks to be given the good of speaking and writing faultless words of Murugan and telling the truth daily. The praise names him Vishnu's nephew, the one who drowned Sura in the seven seas and gave the gods strength, who gave the great truth to Siva, and who is good to the devotees able to keep the poet on the path within knowledge.
1253.nuance: சினமிகுத்த திண்ணர் are likely Death's servants, though the song does not name Yama. நிற்சொல் சொல்லி எழுதி: the plea is for speaking and writing praise, a poet's petition. The last line credits devotees (அடியவர்) with keeping the poet on the path.

1254.reading: In the voice of a love-sick girl, the singer says that the south wind, the pounding sea, the moon scattering fire, the anril bird and the five arrows close in at dusk, and asks the lover to give his garland lovingly so that her heart does not perish. The praise names Murugan whose chest embraces Valli, whose anklets are hung with pearls and bells, whom konrai-wearing Siva once came to worship, and who struck the hill.
1254.nuance: This is akam poetry, not the poet's confession: the request for the hero's garland (அலங்கல்) is the heroine's classical plea. The machinery is that of 24: wind, sea, moon, anril and Kama's arrows at evening.

1255.reading: The poet vows that whether he lives as a king, with drums at a festooned golden gate, young women waving chowries, bards praising his arms and elephants, chariots, banners and horses filling the land, or whether poverty grows, he will speak of nothing but Murugan's feet. The praise names him the cause of the worlds, adorned by the hill-like breasts of the hunter girl, scourge of the asuras who resettled the gods' king in his city, who frightened Brahma and rides the peacock, with supreme wisdom, beauty and manliness.
1255.nuance: There is no confession and no request: வாழினும் வறுமை கூரினும் ... ஒழிய மொழியேனே is a vow of constancy in either fortune. The royal pomp is described at length only to be set aside.

1256.reading: The poet confesses giving his mind willingly to women who strike with poison-sword eyes and covet wealth, a dam built in the conch-filled sea, and asks whether a day will come when he, a wretch packed with shame, will think of Murugan so that the seven troubled births leave and the books he learned rejoice. The praise names him Vishnu's nephew, the young one who crushed the long hill in the sea, and the one who took up the vel to stand beside the hunter woman with pearl-hung breasts and cutting eyes.
1256.nuance: தனத்தை நத்துவார் may mean 'who covet wealth' or refer to breasts; the reading of courtesans rests on that word. கற்ற நூல் உகக்க: the poet's learning is shamed by his life and would be fulfilled by thinking of the Lord. The marker before ளையோனே has lost a syllable.

1257.reading: The poet describes women with flower-decked, fragrant hair who enchant with poison eyes and speak desires, their minds set on wealth, and asks whether, instead of wasting daily in infatuation with them, a day will come when Murugan gives the true grace of his small lotus feet fragrant with vetchi and kadamba. The praise names him the son of Rudra, the Kumara who uprooted the false Jains spread in all directions and spread the holy ash, the true guru of Siva, and the one who set the mark of his spear on the chest of discus-bearing Vishnu.
1257.nuance: பொய்ச் சமணை வேர் அறுத்து நல் திருநீறே பரப்பி: Murugan identified with Sambandar, who drove out the Jains and spread the holy ash. சக்ரதரன் மார்பகத்தில் சத்தி அடையாளம் இட்ட, the vel's mark on Vishnu's chest, is an allusion I cannot identify.

1258.reading: The poet lists what women show, their hair-line like serpents, bodiced breasts, marked foreheads, cosmetics, dark eyes, cloud-black hair and lily-scented mouths, until he would ride the madal and falls upon those who drag out his life, and asks Murugan to show the lamp of Vedanta to end this rogue's darkness of delusion. The praise is a chain of 'hail': to his lone valour, his blue steed, his kadamba garland, his twelve arms that toppled the seven hills, his generosity that gives what anyone asks; he defeated Sura and guarded Indra's starry world.
1258.nuance: The refrain காட்டி, 'showing', runs through both halves: the women show their bodies, and the poet asks the Lord to show (காட்டி) the lamp of Vedanta instead. மடல் ஊர, to ride the palmyra horse, is the akam lover's public last resort, here turned on the poet himself. போற்றி is the praise's refrain.

1259.reading: Melting like wax in fire before women with musk-scented, flower-decked hair and carp-eyes that fight like weapons by their earrings, the poet asks Murugan to end the suffering in which the two deeds torment him and he loses strength and sense. The praise names him younger brother of the elephant-faced one, the hero whose golden arms embrace Valli, and the six-faced one who fought with the vel while drums sounded and countless ghosts danced.

1260.reading: The poet seems to confess going to vel-eyed women for money, losing his settled hold like a weed in a crop, and the pride of learned verse in which the inner self perishes, and asks Murugan to end that trouble, let him hold the feet and grant him the thought of release. The praise names Vishnu who dried the round sea to fight, Siva beyond reach whose great life Murugan is, the vel that struck the long hill in rage, and the Tamil of release that siddhas hold in their minds and praise.
1260.nuance: The song is set in doubled hard consonants (பற்றநெட் டைப்படைத் துட்டிருட் டை...), and most of the first half resists division into words; the reading is a guess at its outline. கவிக் கொட்டம், the arrogance of poets, would make this a confession of the poet's own pride. முத்தித் தமிழ், the Tamil of release, closes the song.

1261.reading: The poet calls himself an impure dog who takes as instruction the deceitful words of women who cheat on their beds, with eyes sharper than Kama's arrows and swords, and asks for the word of wisdom, rising bliss without 'I' and 'mine', that will end his deeds and the beginningless bond that surrounds him. The praise shows Brahma of the Vedas and sacred thread humbled, the hill struck, Sura hunted in the sea, Indra praising and restored, and Murugan garlanding Devayanai and guarding the gods' army.
1261.nuance: தோதகமாய வார்த்தை போதகமாக நோக்கு: the poet takes the women's deceit (தோதகம்) as teaching (போதகம்), a rhyme that is the song's point. யானொடு தானிலா, without I and self, and சூழும் அநாதி, the beginningless that surrounds, point to the Saiva idea of beginningless bondage. A syllable before ருபார்வை is lost.

links.note: Tirumular says people wander off calling this or that the supreme and that going the ordained way stills the mind's 'that or this' (அது இது); 1247 asks to know, without quarrelling with the sects, the Lord beyond he, she and it, this and that.
The Naladiyar's wise see the body as a bubble in pelting rain and resolve to end their wandering; 1252 calls the poet's own life a bubble (புற்புதப் பிராணன்) and asks for the true word instead.
Both are akam laments at dusk with the south wind, the moon, the anril bird and Kama's arrows; 24 is in a mother's voice, 1254 in the girl's own, asking for the hero's garland.

1247 asks to know the Lord who has passed beyond he, she and it in every distance (அவன் இவன் உவன் ... அவள் இவள் உவள் அது இது உது எனும் ஆறு அற்று) and beyond form and the formless. Tirumanthiram 1872 calls the light within the dark neither woman nor man nor neuter (பெண்ணல்ல ஆணல்ல பேடல்ல), unknowable to anyone. Both deny the Lord the categories of gender and grammar; the song adds person and distance, the Tirumanthiram adds that he sees without eyes and hears without ears.

1247 asks to know the Lord without quarrelling (சருவா நின்று) with the many sectarians, ritualists and hair-plucking ascetics. Tirumanthiram 1547, in the chapter on the quarrel of sects, says that if one knows how to gain the light standing within there is no quarrel at all (பிணக்கொன்றும் இல்லை). The song asks for the knowing as the way out of the dispute; the Tirumanthiram states that the dispute ends where that knowing begins.

1248 likens women's breasts to the tusks of a rutting elephant (கடாக் களிற்று உரகோடு), to peaks and to tender coconuts, and confesses wasting nights and days in their net. Kural 1087 says the cloth over a woman's firm breasts is like the face-cloth over a rutting elephant (கடாஅக் களிற்றின்மேற் கட்படாம்). Both use the elephant in rut for the breast's force; in the Kural the cloth restrains it, in the song nothing does and the poet asks to be set to praise instead.

1249 asks that his two deceitful deeds be destroyed as he plunges and plays in the Sivaganga tank (சிவகங்கை தனில் முழுகி விளையாடி), with Sivam leaping into him. Tirumanthiram 509 says the many holy waters are within the heart, and those who do not bathe there so that deeds are destroyed (வினைகெட) wander over hollow and height with deceitful minds. If Sivaganga is the outer tank of Chidambaram, the song asks for the cleansing the Tirumanthiram says outer waters cannot give; if it is an inner water, as the following possession by Sivam may suggest, the two agree.

1250 names the great maya that looks on the leather bag of the five elements as 'I' (தோற்பை யானாக நோக்கும் மா மாயை) and tends a body that ghosts, vultures, jackals and crows will tear (காக்கை பீறா). Tirumanthiram 167 asks what it matters if crows carry off the nest once the dancer who stood in the skin bag (தோற்பையுள் நின்று ... கூத்தன்) has left it. The Tirumanthiram separates the dweller from the bag; the song names the failure to make that separation as the delusion it cannot end.

1250 calls the body a leather bag (தோற்பை) oozing the mire of desire, wrongly taken as oneself, and pictures its tearing by scavengers. Naladiyar 26, in nearly the words of Tirumanthiram 167, asks what it matters whether the body is dragged off with a rope, buried or reviled once the dancer within the skin bag (தோற்பையுள் நின்று) has gone. The ethical and the devotional books share the figure; the song turns it into a confession of still tending the bag.

1251 sets itself against sophist sectarians who rise to argue and plant flag against flag (கொடிக்கொடி எதிர்கூறி), and asks to be wholly the Lord's servant and given the one word that reveals the first principle the Vedas do not know. Tirumanthiram 2515 says there is no need to quarrel (பிணங்கவும் வேண்டாம்): if all agree 'our Lord is the Lord', there love can be had. Both answer the debate of sects by turning from argument to surrender; the song asks for a word, the Tirumanthiram for agreement and love.

1252 calls the poet's life a bubble (புற்புதப் பிராணன்) and asks for the true word Murugan gave Siva. Tirumanthiram 2587 sets the body beside a bubble on flowing water (கழிகின்ற நீரிற் குமிழி), a vanishing shadow-man and camphor in flame, and says it goes into the Supreme. The same figure of transience leads the song to ask for teaching and the Tirumanthiram to describe the body's dissolution into the Supreme.

1253 asks, before the fierce ones (likely Death's servants) close in and break his strength (சினமிகுத்த திண்ணர் ... வன்மை சிதையாமுன்), to be given the good of speaking and writing true words of the Lord daily. Tirumanthiram 255 says Death comes in force (வன்மையில் வந்திடும் கூற்றம்) without asking whether one is good, poor or young, and urges good austerity before it. Both race the same violent end; the Tirumanthiram's remedy is tapas, the song's is praise spoken and written.

1256 confesses that his mind went to women and asks whether a day will come when, thinking of the Lord, the books he learned would rejoice (கற்ற நூல் உகக்க). Kural 2 asks what learning has achieved if the learned do not bow at the good feet of the one of pure knowledge (கற்றதனால் ஆய பயனென்கொல்). The song applies the Kural's verdict to the poet himself: his learning is shamed until it is turned to the Lord.

1257 describes women who enchant with poison eyes, speak many desires (இச்சை பல பேசி) and whose minds crave good wealth (நற்பொருள் அவா மனத்தர்), and asks not to waste away infatuated with them. Kural 911 says the sweet words of women who desire wealth and not the man (அன்பின் விழையார் பொருள்விழையும்) bring harm. The song shows the talk and the craving the Kural names, and the daily wasting (நித்தம் மெலியாதே) that is the harm.

1258 has the poet, shown women's bodies, ready to ride the madal (மடலூர) and falling on those who drag out his life, and asks for the lamp of Vedanta to end that darkness. Kural 1131 says that for those who suffer in love there is no safeguard or strength but the palmyra horse (மடலல்லது இல்லை வலி). The Kural's last resort of a lover becomes in the song a mark of the rogue's delusion (தூர்த்தன் மோகாந்தகாரம்), answered by a lamp rather than a public plea.

1259 melts like wax in fire (எரியுறு மெழுகென) before women whose carp-eyes fight like weapons (படைபொருவன விழிக் கயல்). Naladiyar 44 refuses to be troubled by men who call eyes lilies, fighting carp or spears (பொருகயல் வேல்), and sees an eye as a scooped-out palm fruit. The same comparison that the Naladiyar dismantles is the one the song confesses to have yielded to, asking the Lord to end the suffering it brings.

1261 asks for the word of wisdom, rising bliss without 'I' and self (யானொடு தானிலா), that ends his deeds and the beginningless bond. Kural 346 says one who cuts off the pride of 'I' and 'mine' (யான் எனது என்னும் செருக்கு) enters a world higher than the gods'. Both make the loss of 'I' the gate to release; the song asks for it as a gift of grace after confessing that he took women's deceit for teaching.

source_issues: 1258: ஡ stands for ஊ in மடலூர and ஡ண for ரீ in உயிரீர்வார் (printed மடலு஡ர, உயி஡ணர்வார்).
1253: initial உ is split from its word by a space (உ ள்ள).
1250, 1256, 1261: a syllable is lost before the refrain marker '....... ;' (ளையோனே for இளையோனே in 1250 and 1256; ருபார்வை in 1261).
